summary:
Mars Mission Commander is a playable browser-based learning game developed by plus c for the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge. Players become the commander of a Mars outpost and complete a six-turn mission, balancing oxygen, power, water, food, research, and crew protection. Guided conversations, resource forecasts, and feedback help players understand how each decision affects survival and scientific progress.

The prototype connects gameplay to NASA resources, including MOXIE’s oxygen-production demonstration, archived ISS radiation observations from RadLab, space-plant research from OSD-314, and Perseverance imagery. Scientific evidence is clearly distinguished from fictional game rules.

Our project addresses the challenge by turning space-survival concepts into decisions young explorers can practise. It aims to make the connections between engineering, science, and resource management easier to understand through exploration and experimentation. Its educational impact remains a goal for future learner testing.
details:
Mars Mission Commander is a browser-based educational game in which players become the commander of a Mars outpost. Developed by plus c for the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge, the prototype turns space-survival concepts into decisions players can explore, compare, and learn from.

Players begin with an illustrative Earth-to-Mars arrival and meet Dr. Maya, Alex, and NOVA, a scripted guide. They explore the outpost and inspect facilities such as the power station, life-support unit, greenhouse, science laboratory, and radiation shelter. Across six turns, players allocate electricity, manage oxygen, water, and food, and choose a crew task. Tasks include research, rover sampling, sheltering, improving shielding, requesting delayed Earth advice, or conserving power.

Before committing a turn, players can compare predicted resource changes and revise their plan. Resources are spent only when they select Advance turn. The game then explains the outcome, making trade-offs visible: producing oxygen costs electricity, growing food requires power and water, and sheltering protects the crew while using an opportunity for research. A final debrief connects decisions to crew safety, scientific progress, and remaining supplies.

NASA resources give these choices scientific context. MOXIE informs the oxygen-production explanation; archived ISS radiation observations support the radiation chart; OSD-314 research informs the plant-lighting lesson; and Perseverance imagery provides geological context. The game clearly separates this evidence from its fictional resource rates, exposure points, event schedule, and growth times.

The intended benefit is to help young explorers understand that space missions involve connected systems and competing priorities. Rather than memorising isolated facts, players practise planning, interpreting forecasts, and explaining consequences. Potential settings include classrooms, science clubs, and family learning. These are intended benefits; educational effectiveness still needs testing with learners.

Our development tools included:

  • React, TypeScript, and Vite for the application and interface.
  • Three.js, React Three Fiber, and Drei for the interactive 3D environment.
  • Blender and Python for procedural models and asset preparation.
  • Zod and browser local storage for validating and saving mission progress.
  • Vitest, Playwright, and ESLint for automated checks and code quality.
  • GitHub and Vercel for source management and publishing.
  • Miro for brainstorming, mapping the player journey, and connecting ideas about crew, facilities, resources, and consequences.
  • OpenAI Codex for AI-assisted development and documentation; ElevenLabs, Whisper, and FFmpeg for demo narration, caption alignment, and video production.

The project’s creativity comes from combining an explorable outpost, character-guided storytelling, and a decision-based resource model. Scientific explanations appear alongside relevant actions, allowing players to connect evidence with the choices they make.

Our team considered scientific accuracy, clear language, manageable complexity, accessibility, performance, and honest representation of progress. The prototype includes keyboard and touch controls, reduced-motion support, lower rendering quality, an alternative 2D mission map, and replayable guidance. Further work includes supervised learner testing, broader device and browser checks, and manual accessibility evaluation.
